title: How video compression shrinks films
examples: How is video compressed for streaming?

explain.say: A film is a stream of still pictures, often 30 every second. Stored raw, one second of full HD video is about 1,500 megabits, far too much to stream over a home internet connection.
Compression shrinks it hundreds of times, so HD streaming needs only about 5 megabits a second. It works because most of each frame is almost the same as the one before.

The video starts with one complete keyframe. For the next frames, the encoder splits the picture into blocks and records which way each block moved, called motion vectors, plus any small changes left over.

stages.note: One complete picture every second or two.

stages.label: Motion vectors
stages.note: Later frames say which blocks moved where.

stages.label: Small changes
stages.note: Only the leftover differences are stored.

stages.label: Drop fine detail
stages.note: Detail your eye barely notices is thrown away.

explain.say: Encoders also throw away fine detail and subtle colour that our eyes barely notice. This is lossy compression, and it is why fast action or confetti can look blocky when the internet is slow.

faq.a: A keyframe is a complete picture stored in full, usually every second or two. The frames in between only store changes from it, and keyframes let you skip ahead in a video without starting from the beginning.
asks: Why does skipping in a video take a moment?

faq.a: Motion vectors are little arrows saying a block of the picture moved from here to there since the last frame. Sending an arrow is far cheaper than sending the pixels all over again.
asks: How does video compression handle moving things?

faq.a: Lossy compression throws away information people are unlikely to notice, such as tiny details and slight colour differences. The file becomes much smaller, but the lost detail cannot be got back.
asks: What is the difference between lossy and lossless?

faq.a: When the internet slows, the stream drops to a lower data rate, so the encoder must throw away more detail. Fast-changing scenes like confetti or water need the most data, so they break into visible blocks first.
asks: Why does my stream look pixelated?

faq.a: A codec is the method, and the software or chip, that encodes and decodes video. Common ones are H.264, HEVC and AV1; newer codecs give the same quality using less data.

facts: Uncompressed 1080p video at 30 frames per second with 24-bit colour needs about 1.5 gigabits per second.
The HEVC (H.265) codec typically needs about half the data of H.264 for similar picture quality.
